panels.rationale: Slit-lamp photograph of a real patient's left eye showing complete crystalline lens dislocation with diffuse corneal stromal edema. Ectopia lentis is the classic ocular manifestation of classical homocystinuria, and the article title and in-text mention confirm the diagnosis. The dislocation here is into the anterior chamber (rather than the more common inferior direction), so the precise direction and the corneal edema are recorded as proposed findings.
panels.attribution_text: Miraftabi et al. Unilateral and Spontaneous Complete Anterior Dislocation of the Crystalline Lens in a Patient With Homocystinuria.. Cureus 2021. doi:10.7759/cureus.14655. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Complete dislocation of the crystalline lens into the anterior chamber accompanied with diffuse corneal stromal edema in the left eye.
in_text_mentions: f the patient’s poor cooperation. The fixation behavior of the right eye appeared normal, but the left eye could fixate without following the target. Due to corneal haziness and complete lens dislocation into the anterior chamber, the determination of the refractive error in this eye was not possible. The previous records indicated the cyclorefraction of the left eye was -12.50/-3.50×90⸰. The relative afferent pupillary defect was absent. Slit-lamp examination revealed a dislocation of the crystalline lens into the anterior chamber with diffuse corneal stromal edema in the left eye (Figure 2).

A: Non-contrast cranial CT of a boy later confirmed to have classic homocystinuria (elevated homocysteine/methionine), showing a hyperdense cortical vein over the right parietal convexity - the acute cerebral venous thrombosis at presentation described in the article title and caption. B: Brain MRI of the same boy with biochemically confirmed classic homocystinuria showing extensive white matter changes; the in-text description notes abnormal T2 prolongation diffusely throughout the white matter of both hemispheres, corpus callosum, anterior commissure and internal capsule. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Transthoracic echo (parasternal long-axis with color Doppler) of the patient showing mitral regurgitation and a dilated left ventricle. DCM is documented in this article as a rare presentation of hyperhomocysteinemia/classical homocystinuria, but it is a recognized complication rather than a classic hallmark finding, and no matching vocabulary finding_key exists, so confidence is moderate. B: Apical four-chamber transthoracic echo with color Doppler of the same patient demonstrating mitral regurgitation jet and left ventricular dilation attributable to the hyperhomocysteinemia-associated dilated cardiomyopathy reported in the article; no vocabulary finding_key covers cardiac manifestations.

in_text_mentions: anch occlusion but revealed partial thrombus in the subclavian vein with multiple collateral vessels in the left lower neck and upper back. There was a minor filling defect in the left ventricle suspicious for a thrombus (Figure 3). A formal two-dimensional ECHO with color Doppler confirmed POCUS findings and quantified severely diminished systolic function with an ejection fraction at 10% along with left ventricular wall thinning (Figure 4). An attempt to view the intraventricular thrombus with contrast was inconclusive because the examination was suboptimal due to a marked swirling artifact.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal CTA of the chest in a patient diagnosed with hyperhomocysteinemia (classical homocystinuria) showing a partially occluding left subclavian vein thrombus; thromboembolism is a classic manifestation of classical homocystinuria and is the primary radiologic finding captioned for this panel. B: Sagittal CTA with an arrow pointing to an intraventricular filling defect suspicious for thrombus in the same hyperhomocysteinemia patient; intracardiac thrombus falls within the thrombophilic manifestations of classical homocystinuria, though cardiac thrombus is a less common site. C: Axial CTA of the chest with an arrow marking the intraventricular filling defect in the left ventricle, corroborating the thrombus seen in panel B in this patient with hyperhomocysteinemia-associated thrombophilia.
